Stop 0 · Reading the notation
2 concepts · about 10 min

Goal: Recognize the units and order-of-magnitude notation used everywhere, so formulas read smoothly.

Almost every result in the paper is stated up to order (≲, ≍), and bits and nats are converted back and forth. A few minutes here make every later formula easier to read.

Step 1

Risk order风险量级

Core concepts of the paper

Results are stated up to order; learning to read ≲ and ≍ makes every theorem readable at a glance.

Rigorous explanation
For positive a,b, a≲b means a≤Cb for a constant C independent of (N,m,n); a≳b likewise; a≍b means both. Constants may depend on the model, the dimension d, the per-processor bit count k, and assumption constants (v,b,L). a∨b=max{a,b}. Since max{x,y}≤x+y≤2max{x,y}, "maximum" and "sum" are equivalent up to ≍.
Plain explanation

Only how the risk scales with N,m,n, not the constants.

a≲b means a≤Cb with C independent of N,m,n; a≍b means both directions. Constants may depend on the model, d and k, so results are rate statements, not sharp constants.

Step 2

Nat纳特

Information theory

Communication is counted in bits, entropy in nats; they differ by ln 2 — the source of B ln 2.

Rigorous explanation
Bits use log2​, nats use ln: 1bit=ln2nat. A random variable with values in a set of size M satisfies H(T)≤lnM; a transcript with at most 2B values has H(T)≤Bln2 (see Eq. (10)).
Plain explanation

Unit of information with natural logarithms; 1 bit = ln2≈0.693 nats.

Bits use log2​, nats use ln. Entropies in the paper are in nats, so a B-bit transcript has entropy at most H(T)≤ln(2B)=Bln2.

Stop 1 · Estimation and risk
8 concepts · about 40 min

Goal: Understand how estimation quality is measured: squared error, worst case, Bayesian average.

The paper asks how small the error can be. This stop connects error, worst case and average case, and introduces the Gaussian running example.

Step 3

Estimator估计器

Statistics basics

Start from the basics: what are we estimating, and from what?

Rigorous explanation
Here an estimator is a measurable map of the fusion center whose inputs are only the transcript T, the public design S and the public seed R0​; raw observations are invisible to the fusion center.
Plain explanation

A rule that maps what you observe to a guess of the parameter.

An estimator is a function of the data that outputs a guess θ of the unknown θ. Here the fusion center only sees bits, so the estimator has the form θ=δ(T,S,R0​).

Its quality is measured by the squared error ∥θ−θ∥2.

Step 4

Squared-error risk平方误差风险

Statistics basics

Given an estimator, measure how good it is: squared error.

Rigorous explanation
Loss is squared Euclidean distance ℓ(θ,θ)=∥θ−θ∥22​=∑j=1d​(θj​−θj​)2; risk is its expectation Eθ​∥θ−θ∥2, taken over the pool, the random design S and the protocol randomness. By additivity, coordinate errors add without requiring independence.
Plain explanation

The expected squared distance between the estimate and the truth.

Eθ​∥θ−θ∥2=j=1∑d​Eθ​(θj​−θj​)2.

It is a sum over coordinates, so coordinate errors add up without any independence assumption.

Intuition: with n independent samples, estimating a mean costs about 1/n in squared error. All "rates" in the paper are of this kind.

Step 5

Minimax risk极小极大风险

CoreStatistics basics

Squared error depends on the true parameter, so ask how well one can do in the worst case — the quantity studied here.

Rigorous explanation
For a protocol class A∈{NI,BB}, the random-design minimax risk is Since noninteractive protocols are special blackboard protocols, so it suffices to lower-bound RBB​ and upper-bound RNI​.
Plain explanation

Let an adversary pick the hardest parameter, then use your best scheme: the worst-case error of the best scheme.

R=schemesinf​ θ∈Θsup​ Eθ​∥θ−θ∥2.

Read it inside out: for each scheme, look at its worst θ (sup); then choose the best scheme (inf).

A "scheme" here is the whole system: how each processor encodes its bits plus how the fusion center decodes. So R is a fundamental limit of the communication system, not the performance of one algorithm.

"Random design" means the expectation also averages over the randomly drawn subsets.

Self-check: Why can a lower bound be proved via the Bayes risk?
Because the worst case ≥ the average under any prior: supθ​≥∫⋅π(θ)dθ. If the Bayes risk cannot be small, neither can the minimax risk.
Next: Prior distribution →
Step 6

Prior distribution先验分布

Statistics basics

Worst cases are hard to handle directly; for lower bounds, put a distribution on the parameter.

Rigorous explanation
The converse uses the product prior where h(π) is the differential entropy and Jπ​=∫∥∇logπ∥2π the prior Fisher information. It vanishes on ∂[0,1]d, so integration by parts in van Trees has no boundary terms.
Plain explanation

A distribution placed on the unknown parameter; here only a proof device.

The paper uses the product prior π(θ)=j=1∏d​2sin2(πθj​),θ∈[0,1]d.

It vanishes on the boundary of the cube (no boundary terms in integration by parts), and its Fisher information Jπ​=4π2d and differential entropy h(π)=d(ln2−1) are explicit.

Step 7

Bayes risk贝叶斯风险

Statistics basics

A prior gives an average error, and average ≤ worst — the first key to lower bounds.

Rigorous explanation
Given a prior π, the Bayes risk is D=E∥θ(Y)−Θ∥2 with Θ∼π. For any estimator, so every Bayes-risk lower bound is a minimax lower bound.
Plain explanation

The error averaged over a prior on the parameter. Average ≤ worst case, so it lower-bounds the minimax risk.

θsup​Eθ​∥θ−θ∥2 ≥ ∫Eθ​∥θ−θ∥2π(θ)dθ.

The standard route to a lower bound: pick a convenient prior π and show that even the Bayes risk cannot be small.

Step 8

Conditional expectation条件期望

Probability tools

The score identity and data processing both rest on conditional expectation.

Rigorous explanation
E[Y∣T] is the σ(T)-measurable variable with E[(Y−E[Y∣T])g(T)]=0 for all bounded measurable g — the orthogonal projection of Y in L2 onto σ(T)-measurable functions. By conditional Jensen, E∥E[Y∣T]∥2≤E∥Y∥2.
Plain explanation

The best average guess of a quantity given partial information.

E[Y∣T] is the best mean-square predictor of Y from T. Key property: E(E[Y∣T])2≤EY2 (conditional Jensen) — the origin of the data-processing inequality.

Step 9

Posterior law后验分布

SkimStatistics basics

After seeing the transcript, how does our knowledge of the data update?

Rigorous explanation
Given Y=y, the conditional law of the parameter (or of a data block) is the posterior. In Section III-C, by the rectangle property, given T=t (and the seeds) the law of each block Zi​ is its prior law restricted to {Zi​∈Ei​(t)} and renormalized, and blocks are conditionally independent; the posterior mean Eθ​[Ai​∣T=t] is the conditional score mean on an event.
Plain explanation

Updated knowledge about an unknown after seeing the data (here, the transcript).

In Section III-C, once the full transcript t is fixed, the posterior law of each processor's block depends only on its own constraint Ei​(t) — a consequence of the rectangle property. The posterior mean E[Ai​∣T=t] is the average block score given the bits.

Step 10

Gaussian mean estimation高斯均值估计

Statistics basics

A running example to test every concept against.

Rigorous explanation
Model X∼Nd​(θ,Id​), θ∈[0,1]d. Score ξθ​(x)=x−θ∼N(0,Id​) satisfies (19) with v=1,b=0; IX​(θ)=Id​. Bounded moment ψj​(x)=1{xj​≥0}, μj​(θ)=Φ(θj​), inverse-Lipschitz constant L=φ(1)−1 (Section V-A). Section III-E ends with an explicit lower bound for this model, Eq. (230).
Plain explanation

Data X∼Nd​(θ,Id​); estimate the mean. The running example.

The score is ξθ​(x)=x−θ∼N(0,I), so v=1, b=0, and I(θ)=Id​.

With q independent samples and no communication limit, the best squared error is about d/q. Plug this example into every statement to check intuition.

Stop 2 · Probability toolbox
11 concepts · about 45 min

Goal: Collect the small tools used in the proofs: independence, moments, tails, inequalities.

Both proofs use a set of probability tools. No need to master them at once — know what each is for and come back when needed.

Step 11

Conditional independence条件独立性

Probability tools

Both proofs rely on fixing something so that the rest becomes independent.

Rigorous explanation
X,Y are conditionally independent given Z if P(X∈A,Y∈B∣Z)=P(X∈A∣Z)P(Y∈B∣Z) a.s. Two key instances: (i) given the full transcript t and seeds, blocks are independent (Eq. (150), rectangle property); (ii) given the shared observations G and the design, private blocks Vi​ are independent (Eq. (172)).
Plain explanation

Variables that become independent once something else is known.

Two key instances:
  • Converse: given the full transcript, processors' blocks remain independent (rectangle property).
  • Achievability: given the whole pool, resampled observations of different processors are independent (exact resampling).

Step 12

Jensen / Cauchy–SchwarzJensen 不等式

Probability tools

Two everyday inequalities used in van Trees and data processing.

Rigorous explanation
Jensen: for convex f, f(EX)≤Ef(X), also conditionally. Cauchy–Schwarz: E⟨X,Y⟩≤(E∥X∥2)1/2(E∥Y∥2)1/2. van Trees applies Cauchy–Schwarz to E⟨θ−Θ,Q⟩=d:
Plain explanation

The everyday wrenches of the proofs.

  • Jensen: for convex f, f(EX)≤Ef(X), e.g. (EX)2≤EX2.
  • Cauchy–Schwarz: E⟨X,Y⟩≤E∥X∥2​E∥Y∥2​; the van Trees inequality rests on it.
  • Triangle: ∥x+y∥≤∥x∥+∥y∥ and ∥x+y∥2≤2∥x∥2+2∥y∥2.

Step 13

Integration by parts分部积分

SkimProbability tools

The one calculus trick inside van Trees; just know it.

Rigorous explanation
∫01​fg′dt=[fg]01​−∫01​f′gdt. In van Trees, integrating by parts in θj​ — with π zero on the boundary and ∂θj​​(θj​(y)−θj​)=−1 — gives
Plain explanation

∫fg′=[fg]−∫f′g; boundary terms vanish because the prior is zero on the boundary.

The key computation in van Trees: integrating by parts in θj​ gives E[(θj​−Θj​)Qj​]=1, because θj​ does not depend on θ and ∂θj​​(θj​−θj​)=−1.

Step 14

Moment-generating function矩母函数

Probability tools

To describe how heavy tails are, we need the MGF.

Rigorous explanation
MGF MX​(t)=EetX; cumulant (log-MGF) ΛX​(t)=logMX​(t) with Λ′(0)=EX, Λ′′(0)=VarX. The characteristic function φX​(t)=EeitX always exists. Section IV-C uses the binomial characteristic function Ft​(p)=(1−p+peit)m (Eq. (304)).
Plain explanation

EetX (MGF) or EeitX (characteristic function) packs a whole distribution into one function.

The log-MGF describes tails (sub-Gaussian / Bernstein conditions are bounds on it).

The characteristic function always exists. Section IV-C uses Ft​(p)=(1−p+peit)m for a binomial count; its phase rotates with p, and one bit can measure its real or imaginary part.

Step 15

Sub-Gaussian次高斯

Probability tools

Use the MGF to define tails as light as a Gaussian's.

Rigorous explanation
A zero-mean Y is sub-Gaussian with variance factor v if logEetY≤vt2/2 for all t∈R; for vectors, along every direction u⊤Y. Equivalent (up to constants) to tails P(∣Y∣≥x)≤2e−x2/(2v). It is the case b=0 of assumption (19).
Plain explanation

Tails at least as light as a Gaussian's.

logEetY≤2vt2​ for all real t (zero-mean Y).

It is the b=0 case of the score condition (19). Gaussian means, Bernoulli away from the boundary, multinomial, logistic regression satisfy it.

Step 16

Hoeffding inequalityHoeffding 不等式

SkimProbability tools

Bounded variables are automatically sub-Gaussian — handy for checking assumptions.

Rigorous explanation
Hoeffding's lemma: if Y∈[α,β] and EY=0, then logEetY≤t2(β−α)2/8, i.e. Y is (β−α)2/4-sub-Gaussian; this yields Hoeffding's inequality for sums. The bounded-score criterion of Section V, Eq. (379), is exactly this: ∥ξθ​∥≤M⇒ (19) with v=M2,b=0.
Plain explanation

Averages of bounded independent variables concentrate exponentially fast.

For independent Yi​∈[−1,1], P(∣Yˉ−EYˉ∣≥ϵ)≤2e−rϵ2/2. Hoeffding's lemma: a variable with range of length ℓ is ℓ2/4-sub-Gaussian. Used to verify score conditions and to control one-bit measurements.

Step 17

Bernoulli observations伯努利观测

Statistics basics

Key step of the upper bound: any bounded statistic becomes a coin.

Rigorous explanation
If ψj​(X)∈[0,1] and V∼Unif[0,1] is independent, then so any bounded moment becomes, through private randomization, a Bernoulli observation with success probability equal to the target moment.
Plain explanation

0/1 random variables equal to 1 with probability p.

If ψ(X)∈[0,1] and V is an independent uniform variable, then U=1{V≤ψ(X)} satisfies P(U=1)=Eψ(X).

So any bounded statistic can be randomized into a coin whose success probability is the target moment; every model reduces to estimating coin probabilities.

Step 18

Binomial count二项计数

Statistics basics

Many coins add up to a binomial count.

Rigorous explanation
K=∑l=1m​Ul​ with Ul​∼iidBernoulli(p) gives K∼Bin(m,p), EK=mp, VarK=mp(1−p)≤m/4. In Section IV, after resampling and randomization each processor holds a binomial count (conditionally independent given the pool) with parameter the pool moment pN,j​.
Plain explanation

The number of successes among m independent coins, Bin(m,p).

After resampling and randomization, each processor holds a count K∼Bin(m,p). The problem becomes: n processors, each with a binomial count and k bits — estimate p.

Step 19

Empirical moments经验矩

Statistics basics

Averages over the pool always differ from true expectations by about d/(4N).

Rigorous explanation
Empirical moment μN​=N1​∑a=1N​ψ(Xa​) Eq. (25); population moment μ(θ)=Eθ​ψ(X). Since ψj​∈[0,1], Varψj​≤1/4, hence The pool empirical law PN​=N1​∑a​δXa​​ is the target of the resampling in IV-A.
Plain explanation

Averages computed from the sample (empirical) versus expectations under the true law (population).

Pool empirical moment μN​=N1​∑a=1N​ψ(Xa​); population moment μ(θ)=Eθ​ψ(X). Eθ​∥μN​−μ(θ)∥2≤4Nd​.

The achievability scheme first estimates the pool's empirical moment, then pays this extra d/(4N).

Step 20

Sufficient statistic充分统计量

Statistics basics

Why does the classical reduction to sufficient statistics fail under overlap?

Rigorous explanation
S(X) is sufficient for {Pθ​} if the law of X given S(X) does not depend on θ (Fisher–Neyman: pθ​(x)=gθ​(S(x))h(x)). With independent blocks, reducing to local sufficient statistics is lossless; in a shared pool, local data are dependent through shared observations and such a reduction may destroy structure needed for coordinated encoding (Section VI).
Plain explanation

A summary that loses no information about the parameter, e.g. the sample mean for Gaussian means.

With independent blocks, reducing each block to a sufficient statistic is lossless. With overlap this step may lose information: which observations are shared, and what values they take, can be used to coordinate encodings, and per-processor means flatten that structure. This is one reason the intermediate-overlap regime is open (Section VI).

Step 21

Random kernel随机核

SkimProbability tools

Abstract a protocol as a parameter-free random rule.

Rigorous explanation
A random (Markov) kernel K(⋅∣z) is a probability law in t for each z, measurable in z. A protocol is a kernel that does not depend on θ, so the transcript law is
Plain explanation

A rule that produces a random output from an input, without depending on the parameter.

An encoding protocol is a kernel K(t∣z). Because K does not know θ, all information about θ in T comes from the data — which is why the score identity holds.

Stop 3 · Score and Fisher information
6 concepts · about 45 min

Goal: Understand how much information data carry about the parameter, and the per-observation cap.

The protagonist of the converse is Fisher information. This stop goes from the score to "compression only loses information".

Step 22

Regularity正则性

SkimStatistics basics

Before Fisher information, make sure the model is smooth enough.

Rigorous explanation
Regularity for the converse (Section II-B): {Pθ​} dominated by ν with common support X0​; θ↦pθ​(x) differentiable in the interior of Θ; square-integrable scores; differentiation under the integral: This guarantees Eθ​ξθ​=0 and the score identity. Nonregular experiments with parameter-dependent support (e.g. Unif[0,θ]) are excluded.
Plain explanation

Technical conditions: support does not move with the parameter, the likelihood is differentiable, derivative and integral commute.

They guarantee that scores have mean zero and Fisher information behaves as usual. Counterexample: models whose support depends on the parameter, such as Uniform[0,θ], can have rate 1/n2; the converse does not cover them.

Step 23

Score得分函数

CoreStatistics basics

The raw material of Fisher information: the gradient of the log-likelihood.

Rigorous explanation
Score and single-observation Fisher information: Under regularity Eθ​ξθ​(X)=0 and Covθ​ξθ​(X)=IX​(θ).
Plain explanation

Gradient of the log-likelihood: how fast the likelihood of an observation changes when the parameter moves.

ξθ​(x)=∇θ​logpθ​(x),Eθ​ξθ​(X)=0.

A large score means the observation is sensitive to θ and helps distinguish nearby parameters. Its mean is zero and its covariance is the Fisher information.

Example: for X∼N(θ,1), ξθ​(x)=x−θ.

Step 24

Fisher information费舍尔信息

CoreStatistics basics

The central object of the converse — how much information the data carry.

Rigorous explanation
For an experiment Y∼PθY​, JY​(θ)=Eθ​[∇logpθY​(Y)∇logpθY​(Y)⊤]. Properties: (i) additive over independent data, JX1​,…,Xq​​=qIX​; (ii) data-processing monotonicity JT​⪯JZ​ Eq. (79); (iii) chain rule Eq. (83); (iv) under (19), IX​(θ)⪯vId​ and trIX​≤dv Eq. (22). The converse is built around trJT,S,R​ of the transcript.
Plain explanation

How much information the data carry about the parameter; achievable error ≈ 1 / information.

I(θ)=Eθ​[ξθ​(X)ξθ​(X)⊤].
  • Additive over independent observations: q observations give qI(θ).
  • Monotone under processing: compressing data into bits cannot increase it, JT​⪯JZ​.
  • Error ≈ 1/information: Cramér–Rao / van Trees turn an information upper bound into an error lower bound.

Example: one N(θ,1) sample has information 1; q samples give q, error ≈ 1/q.

The whole converse is an upper bound on the Fisher information carried by the transcript.

Step 25

Block score样本块得分

Statistics basics

Add the scores of a block; Lemmas 1 and 3 revolve around it.

Rigorous explanation
For q independent observations the block score is Aq​=∑a=1q​ξθ​(Xa​) Eq. (119). By (19) and independence its log-MGF satisfies i.e. Aq​ obeys a Bernstein bound with variance factor qv and scale b.
Plain explanation

The sum Aq​ of the scores of a block of q independent observations.

Aq​=a=1∑q​ξθ​(Xa​).

Scores of independent observations add, and so do their variances, so the variance factor of the block score is vq. Section III-B asks how large the conditional mean of Aq​ can be when we only learn that an event E occurred.

Bernstein condition伯恩斯坦条件

Probability tools

The paper's only distributional assumption on scores; it also gives information ≤ v per observation.

Rigorous explanation
Score assumption: for all u∈Rd with b∥u∥<1, b=0 is the sub-Gaussian case. A second-order expansion at u=0 gives Eq. (21), hence
Plain explanation

Weaker than sub-Gaussian: allows exponential-type tails, only quadratic near the origin.

Step 27

Data-processing inequality数据处理不等式

CoreInformation theory

First key fact: compressing to bits only loses information.

Rigorous explanation
If T is produced from Z by a θ-free kernel, the score identity ST​=Eθ​[SZ​∣T] and conditional Jensen give (Loewner order). Information-theoretic version: for a Markov chain Θ→Z→T, I(Θ;T)≤I(Θ;Z).
Plain explanation

Processing data (independently of the parameter) cannot create information.

Fisher-information version: if T is produced from Z by a parameter-free kernel, JT​(θ)⪯JZ​(θ).

Proof: score identity ST​=E[SZ​∣T] plus conditional Jensen.

Stop 4 · Information theory
5 concepts · about 40 min

Goal: Bits, entropy, mutual information: what the communication budget really limits.

Communication limits are really limits on entropy. This stop links bits, entropy, mutual information and differential entropy.

Step 28

Entropy熵

CoreInformation theory

Into information theory: bits limit entropy.

Rigorous explanation
Discrete entropy H(T)=−∑t​p(t)lnp(t); conditional entropy H(T∣R)=ER​H(T∣R=r); H(T)≤ln∣T∣. For every protocol, Chain rule H(T,G)=H(G)+H(T∣G); conditioning reduces entropy, H(T∣G,R)≤H(T∣R).
Plain explanation

Uncertainty / maximal information content. With 2B possible messages, entropy ≤ Bln2.

H(T)=−∑t​p(t)lnp(t); H(T∣R) is the remaining uncertainty of T once R is known.

Entropy is the communication budget: B=nk bits give H(T)≤Bln2. The converse shows that each nat of entropy can carry only a limited amount of Fisher information.

Step 29

Self-information自信息

SkimInformation theory

Entropy averages self-information; Lemma 2 controls its second moment.

Rigorous explanation
Self-information ι(t)=lnpT​(t)1​, with H(T)=Eι(T). Lemma 2: if T takes at most 2B values, This second moment only enters the Bernstein correction for b>0.
Plain explanation

How surprising a specific outcome is: lnp(t)1​. Entropy is its average.

Lemma 2: individual outcomes may be very rare, but with at most 2B values the second moment is controlled: Eln2pT​(T)1​≤KB​=(Bln2)2+2Bln2+2.

It only enters the Bernstein (b>0) correction, which is later shown to be harmless.

Step 30

Mutual information互信息

Information theory

Mutual information measures what the transcript tells about the parameter — at most the number of bits.

Rigorous explanation
I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y)=D(PXY​∥PX​PY​) (differential entropy in the continuous case). In Section III-A, with side information W=(S,R): so the parameter–transcript mutual information never exceeds the number of bits.
Plain explanation

How much observing Y reduces uncertainty about X: I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X∣Y).

It never exceeds the entropy of the message: I(Θ;T)≤H(T)≤Bln2 — "B bits tell you at most B bits".

Keep two notions apart: Fisher information (local sensitivity to small parameter changes) and mutual information / entropy (global capacity). The converse connects them.

Step 31

Differential entropy微分熵

Information theory

Uncertainty about a continuous parameter: it turns small error into a large information requirement.

Rigorous explanation
h(X)=−∫plnp. Under a trace constraint on the covariance the Gaussian maximizes differential entropy, hence h(Θ∣Y)≤2d​ln(2πeD/d) Eq. (110). With I(Θ;T,W)=h(π)−h(Θ∣T,W),
Plain explanation

Entropy of a continuous variable; the more concentrated, the smaller (can be negative).

h(X)=−∫plnp. For a fixed variance the Gaussian maximizes it.

It turns "small error D" into "small posterior uncertainty", which requires enough mutual information:

I(Θ;T,W) ≥ h(π)−2d​ln(2πeD/d).

Mutual information is limited by the bits, hence D≳d2−2B/d.

Step 32

Total variation distance全变差距离

SkimInformation theory

How alike two laws are; used for the Gaussian approximation in the upper bound.

Rigorous explanation
Total variation TV(P,Q)=supE​∣P(E)−Q(E)∣=21​∫∣p−q∣; relative entropy (KL) D(P∥Q)=∫plnqp​. Pinsker: TV≤D/2​. Section IV-B uses a TV bound to replace Gaussian inputs by smoothed binomial statistics (Lemma 5, Eq. (263)).
Plain explanation

How different two distributions are. TV = the largest probability gap over events; relative entropy = KL divergence.

TV(P,Q)=Esup​∣P(E)−Q(E)∣.

Small TV means the two laws are almost indistinguishable, so an algorithm designed for one works for the other. Section IV-B uses it to show a smoothed binomial statistic is nearly Gaussian. Pinsker's inequality converts KL into TV.

Step 33

Distributed estimation分布式估计

The model

Tools ready — on to the problem itself.

Rigorous explanation
Model: n processors randomly access m observations each from a shared i.i.d. pool, communicate with a fusion center under a k-bit constraint, and the goal is random-design minimax estimation of θ∈[0,1]d. The fundamental difference from the independent-block model is that local data are dependent through shared observations.
Plain explanation

Data spread over many machines, each sending few bits to a center that estimates the parameter.

The classical setup gives each machine its own independent block. Here machines draw subsets of one shared pool, so their data may overlap: more machines mean more communication, but not necessarily more independent data.

Step 34

Observation pool观测池

CoreThe model

Where everything starts: all machines share one pool.

Rigorous explanation
Observation pool: Parameter space Θ=[0,1]d. The pool size N gives an irreducible statistical lower bound d/N (from Eq. (107)).
Plain explanation

N i.i.d. observations X1​,…,XN​ from which all processors draw.

X1​,…,XN​∼iidPθ​.

Two processors drawing index a see the same random variable Xa​, not two copies. However many machines there are, there are at most N independent observations — the origin of the 1/N term.

Step 35

Sampling design抽样设计

CoreThe model

How each machine takes data from the pool.

Rigorous explanation
Processors independently select uniformly random m-subsets: The full design S=(S1​,…,Sn​) is public and independent of the pool and of θ. The number of distinct accessed observations is U(S)=∣⋃i​Si​∣ with EU=N[1−(1−m/N)n]≤min{N,nm} (Eq. (104)).
Plain explanation

Who drew which indices: S=(S1​,…,Sn​); public knowledge.

Each processor independently draws a uniformly random m-subset of [N] (without replacement): P(Si​=A)=(mN​)−1.

The design is public side information, so processors can coordinate around the overlap. It is independent of θ.

CoreThe model

The source of overlap: observations drawn by at least two machines.

Step 38

Private observations / blocks私有观测

The model

The converse split: shared + private.

Rigorous explanation
Given S, let G=(Xa​:Da​≥2) be the shared observations and Vi​=(Xa​:a∈Si​,Da​=1) the private block of processor i, qi​=∣{a∈Si​:Da​=1}∣≤m Eq. (173). Disjoint index sets make G,V1​,…,Vn​ mutually independent (Eq. (172)).
Plain explanation

Observations drawn by exactly one processor; given the shared ones, private blocks are independent.

Converse decomposition: each processor's data = private block Vi​ + its part of G. Reveal G to everyone; the remaining private blocks are independent and the independent-block method (Lemma 3) applies.

Step 39

Fusion center融合中心

The model

Where data go: the fusion center sees only bits.

Rigorous explanation
The fusion center receives T, knows S and R0​, and outputs θ=δ(T,S,R0​) Eq. (11). In the converse, the private seeds and shared observations may additionally be revealed to it; this only lowers the risk, so lower bounds for the enhanced problem apply to the original.
Plain explanation

The center that receives all bits and outputs the estimate; it never sees raw data.

It sees the transcript T, the public design S, and the public seed R0​, and outputs θ=δ(T,S,R0​).

Step 40

Public / private seeds随机种子

The model

Protocols may use randomness, which carries no parameter information.

Rigorous explanation
The public seed R0​ and private seeds R1​,…,Rn​ are mutually independent and independent of the pool, the design and θ. Write R=(R0​,…,Rn​). Given (S,R) a protocol is a deterministic binary decision tree of depth at most B.
Plain explanation

Random numbers a protocol may use; independent of data and parameter.

Seeds are independent of everything else. In the converse the private seeds can be revealed to the fusion center for free: more information only lowers the risk, so a lower bound for the enhanced problem holds for the original.

Step 41

Side information辅助信息

The model

Which information is free and which is not — crucial for the converse.

Rigorous explanation
Parameter-free side information (S,R) can be conditioned on at no cost: H(T∣S,R)≤Bln2. The shared observations G have a θ-dependent law and cannot enter the entropy budget for free; the proof reveals G only in the Fisher-information comparison (chain rule).
Plain explanation

Information everyone gets for free, outside the bit budget — e.g. the design and seeds.

Design S and seeds R are parameter-free and can be conditioned on in the entropy budget. The shared observations G cannot: their law depends on θ. The proof reveals G only when comparing Fisher information. This distinction produces the additive term.

Step 43

Blackboard protocol黑板协议

CoreThe model

Second protocol class: take turns on a shared board (interaction).

Rigorous explanation
Blackboard protocol: at round r the public history determines the speaker who sends with transcript length L≤B=nk Eq. (9). Scheduling and stopping depend only on the public history, so silence or timing cannot carry uncounted information.
Plain explanation

Processors take turns writing bits on a public board everyone can read (interaction).

Later speakers can adapt to earlier bits. Who speaks next and when to stop may depend only on the public history, so silence or timing cannot leak uncounted information.

The lower bound holds for blackboard protocols. Since noninteractive ⊂ blackboard, RBB​≤RNI​; matching bounds mean interaction does not improve the rate.

10 concepts · about 50 min

Goal: Understand Theorem 1: four bottlenecks, surplus s, a gap of r̄ between bounds, the open regime.

With the model in place, the main results: four bottlenecks, the surplus s, the single rˉ gap, and the one open regime.

Step 46

Localization & refinement粗定位与精细估计

CoreCore concepts of the paper

Before the results: bits must first pay for localization.

Rigorous explanation
One processor's m observations give a local estimate with accuracy ≍m−1/2. Locating the parameter in [0,1] to that accuracy needs log2​m​=21​log2​m bits per coordinate; only the remaining bits push the error below single-machine accuracy (refinement). This decomposition is classical (e.g. Cai–Wei); the surplus s quantifies it. Protocols need not separate the two kinds of messages explicitly.
Plain explanation

First spend bits to locate the parameter to single-machine accuracy, then spend the rest to refine.

Analogy: to tell a friend where you are, first name the city (localization), then the street and number (refinement).

One machine with m observations has accuracy ≈1/m​. Locating the parameter in [0,1] to that accuracy costs about log2​m​=21​log2​m bits per coordinate. Those bits only find the location; the remaining bits reduce the error.

Next: Localization surplus →
Step 47

Localization surplus定位余量

CoreCore concepts of the paper

Bits left after the localization fee — the most important parameter of the paper.

Rigorous explanation
Equivalently s appears naturally both in the upper bound (per-coordinate code length) and in the lower bound (cancellation of lnm in the entropy budget, Eq. (203)). Table I is organized by s≤C0​, s≥εn and 1≪s≪n.
Plain explanation

s=B/d−21​log2​m: bits per coordinate left after paying the localization cost.

s=dB​−21​log2​m,s+​=max{s,0}.
  • s≤ const: bits barely suffice to localize; error set by bits, ≈d2−2nk/d.
  • s≥εn: bits are plentiful; error set by data, ≈d/min{N,nm}.
  • 1≪s≪n: the critical window, error ≈d/(ms) or d/N.

Each extra bit of surplus in refinement is worth roughly one more machine's data, giving the term m(1+s+​)d​.

Bit-only risk floor aB​比特风险底线

CoreCore concepts of the paper

With infinite data, how well can B bits do?

Rigorous explanation
aB​=2−2B/d. Lower bound Eq. (114): from I(Θ;T∣W)≤Bln2 and a differential-entropy argument. Relation to the surplus: aB​=2−2s/m.

Step 51

Shared term rˉ

CoreCore concepts of the paper

Where the only gap between the bounds comes from.

Rigorous explanation
Averaged form of Theorem 2 (Eq. (193)): Shared observations contribute dvrˉ additively, so the fourth lower-envelope term is [m(1+s+​)+rˉ]−1. If rˉ≲m(1+s+​), the fourth terms match.
Plain explanation

The extra rˉ in the lower bound: Fisher information of shared observations, entering additively.

Theorem 2 has the shape trJT​≤shareddvr​​+private×entropy4vmH(T∣R)​​+Bernstein2b2KB​​​.

Why "additive" matters: shared observations contribute at most the information of r observations, not "r × entropy".

The price: the fourth lower-envelope term becomes m(1+s+​)+rˉd​ instead of m(1+s+​)d​ — the only gap between the bounds.

Two fully solved families: polynomial growth and exponential rates.

Corollary 2: (a) if m≍nα, N≍nβ (0≤α≤β), then RBB​≍RNI​≍dn−min{β,1+α}. (b) If n1​log2​m→λ∈[0,∞] and N≥m, then −n1​log2​R→min{λ,2k/d} (Eq. (64)–Eq. (72)).

Step 54

Critical window临界窗口

Core concepts of the paper

The subtlest regime: slightly more bits than localization needs.

Rigorous explanation
Critical localization window: s→∞, s/n→0 (so log2​m≈2nk/d and m grows exponentially in n). Then U≍dmax{N−1,(ms)−1}. Solved: N≲ms (R≍d/N) and N≳n2m/s (R≍d/(ms), since rˉ≲ms, Eq. (53)).
Plain explanation

s→∞ but s/n→0: more bits than localization needs, but not enough to use all data.

Then m grows exponentially in n (since 21​log2​m≈nk/d−s), and the upper bound reduces to dmax{N1​,ms1​}.

Solved ends: N≲ms (error d/N) and N≳n2m/s (error d/(ms)). In between is the open intermediate-overlap regime.

Step 56

Score identity得分恒等式

Proof techniques

Into the converse: the score of the bits is a conditional average of the data score.

Rigorous explanation
If T is produced from Z by a θ-free kernel then, under regularity, obtained by differentiating Eq. (17) in θ and dividing by pθT​(t).
Plain explanation

The score of the compressed message equals the conditional mean of the data score given the message.

∇θ​logpθT​(T)=Eθ​[∇θ​logpθZ​(Z)​T].

The message's sensitivity to the parameter is an average of the data's sensitivity, and averaging washes out signal. It implies the data-processing inequality and starts the converse.

Chain rule (Fisher information)链式法则

Proof techniques

Second tool: split joint information into two parts.

Rigorous explanation
For the joint experiment (G,T): with trace form Eq. (84). Section III-D uses it to separate the information of the shared observations, JG​=rIX​, from that of the conditional experiment T∣G.
Plain explanation

Joint information = information in G + information in T once G is known.

JG,T​(θ)=JG​(θ)+EG​JT∣G​(θ;G).

Used to split off the shared observations (JG​=rIX​) from what the private blocks convey through the transcript, so the shared part enters additively.

Step 58

van Trees inequalityvan Trees 不等式

CoreProof techniques

Third tool: turn an information upper bound into an error lower bound.

Rigorous explanation
Let q(θ,y)=π(θ)pθY​(y) and Q=∇θ​logq Eq. (97). Integration by parts gives E⟨θ−Θ,Q⟩=d; Cauchy–Schwarz and E∥Q∥2=Jπ​+EtrJY​(Θ) Eq. (100) yield valid for any (possibly biased) estimator.
Plain explanation

Bayesian Cramér–Rao: error ≥ d2/(average Fisher information + prior information); valid for biased estimators.

E∥θ−Θ∥2 ≥ EΘ∼π​trJY​(Θ)+Jπ​d2​.

Usage: show the transcript carries at most I Fisher information; then the error is at least ≈d2/I. E.g. information ≤ dvmin{N,nm} ⇒ error ≳d/min{N,nm}.

Rectangle property矩形性质

CoreProof techniques

Extend Lemma 1 to interaction and n machines: the rectangle property.

Rigorous explanation
Given seeds R=r, each bit depends only on its sender's data and the public history, so Lemma 3 (rectangle entropy bound for independent blocks of size ≤q): with Eq. (148) when b=0. Cross terms vanish on average by conditional independence (Eq. (157)).
Plain explanation

Fixing the full transcript, the set of inputs producing it is a product (a “rectangle”) of per-processor conditions.

{T=t}=i=1⋂n​{Zi​∈Ei​(t)}.

Even with interaction, each bit constrains only its sender's data. Hence blocks stay independent given t, cross terms cancel on average, and information does not multiply with n. This yields Lemma 3: trJ≲vqH(T∣R).

Step 63

Entropy budget熵预算

CoreCore concepts of the paper

Last piece: the entropy budget cancels ln m and leaves the surplus s.

Rigorous explanation
Under the prior, the transcript entropy beyond the parameter, hT​:=H(T∣Θ,S,R)/d, is constrained by the total bits and by the mutual information needed to convey the parameter (Eq. (116)–Eq. (118)): Combined with van Trees in Section III-E, lnm cancels (Eq. (203)).
Plain explanation

Transcript entropy ≤ Bln2: all information has to squeeze through this bandwidth.

Two lines of the converse:
  1. Fisher information ≲ m×(transcript entropy) + shared term;
  2. entropy ≤ Bln2 minus what is used up conveying the parameter.

Combined with van Trees, lnm cancels exactly and the surplus s remains.

Lower-bound proof map下界证明全景回顾

Milestone

Congratulations — look back at the complete proof chain.

Rigorous explanation
Chain: (19)⇒IX​⪯vId​ ⟶ score identity Eq. (75) ⟶ data processing Eq. (79) ⟶ van Trees Eq. (101) ⟶ elementary bounds Eq. (107), Eq. (115) ⟶ Lemma 1 Eq. (121) ⟶ Lemma 2 Eq. (139) ⟶ rectangle property Eq. (150) and Lemma 3 Eq. (147) ⟶ Theorem 2 Eq. (174)–Eq. (193) ⟶ entropy budget Eq. (118) ⟶ assembly Eq. (197)–Eq. (219) ⟶ RBB​≥cL Eq. (220).
Plain explanation

The whole converse does one thing: upper-bound the Fisher information in the transcript.

  • Where can information come from? Shared observations (at most dvrˉ) + what private blocks pass through the bits.
  • How much can private blocks pass? Each nat of entropy carries about vm (rectangle property + Lemma 1).
  • How much entropy? At most Bln2, minus what conveying the parameter uses.
  • Information → error: van Trees.

You have now read the hardest part of the paper. The optional stop shows how the limit is actually achieved.

Step 67

Exact resampling精确重抽样

CoreCore concepts of the paper

(Optional) First step of the upper bound: wash overlap into independence.

Rigorous explanation
Lemma 4: given S and the history, generate J1​,…,Jm​∈S by then, averaging over S, Given the pool, each processor's XJ​ are i.i.d. from PN​ (Eq. (245)–Eq. (247)).
Plain explanation

Using only your own m indices, generate a sequence that looks like i.i.d. draws with replacement from the whole pool.

Rule (Lemma 4): each previously used index is repeated with probability 1/N; with the remaining probability (N−r)/N, pick uniformly among unused members of your subset.

Averaged over the random subset S, the indices J1​,…,Jm​ are exactly i.i.d. uniform on [N]. Given the pool, all processors' resampled observations are i.i.d. from the empirical law PN​: the overlap is "washed out".

That repeats with probability 1/m, while full-pool sampling repeats with probability 1/N; exact resampling sets the repeat probability to 1/N.
Next: Moment map →
Step 68

Moment map矩映射

CoreCore concepts of the paper

(Optional) Last step of the upper bound: from moments back to parameters.

Rigorous explanation
Bounded identifying moment (24): there is ψ:X→[0,1]d such that μ(θ)=Eθ​ψ(X) is inverse-Lipschitz, ∥θ−θ′∥≤L∥μ(θ)−μ(θ′)∥: Nearest-point decoding Eq. (351) gives ∥θ−θ∥≤2L∥p​−μ(θ)∥ (Eq. (357)).
Plain explanation

A [0,1]d-valued statistic ψ whose mean μ(θ) determines θ stably.

Condition (24): μ(θ)=Eθ​ψ(X),∥θ−θ′∥≤L∥μ(θ)−μ(θ′)∥.

The inverse-Lipschitz part means: close moments ⇒ close parameters, so a good moment estimate gives a good parameter estimate (error inflated by at most L2).

Examples: Bernoulli ψ(x)=x; Poisson ψ(x)=1{x=0}, μ=e−λ; Gaussian mean ψj​(x)=1{xj​≥0}, μj​=Φ(θj​).

Step 69

Smoothing step平滑步骤

Proof techniques

(Optional) Large blocks: make a discrete statistic look Gaussian.

Rigorous explanation
For the mean Uˉ of q Bernoulli variables, with the variance v estimated from an independent second group, define Lemma 5: A has mean p, is sub-Gaussian, and TV(L(A),N(p,1/q))≤Cq−1/2 (Eq. (263)), so it can feed the Cai–Wei robust Gaussian protocol Eq. (258).
Plain explanation

Add a little Gaussian noise to a discrete binomial mean so it becomes close to Gaussian in total variation.

Any lattice law is at TV distance 1 from every Gaussian, so it must be smoothed: v=Uˉ′(1−Uˉ′),A=Uˉ+q1−v​​G.

The noise tops the variance up to about 1/q, so A≈N(p,1/q) with TV ≤Cq−1/2, and the Cai–Wei robust Gaussian protocol (258) applies.

Step 70

One-bit characteristic-function measurement一比特特征函数测量

Proof techniques

(Optional) Small blocks: one bit per machine suffices.

Rigorous explanation
Lemma 6: Q independent Bin(m,p) counts with one bit each achieve E(p​−p)2≤C/(Qm) Eq. (303). The tool is One-bit randomized measurements of ReFt​ and ImFt​ at doubling frequencies localize coarsely (Eq. (325)–Eq. (331)) and then refine at the top frequency (Eq. (332)–Eq. (337)).
Plain explanation

Small blocks: each machine sends one bit, a randomized measurement of Re or Im of Ft​(p)=(1−p+peit)m.

Ft​(p) is a complex number whose phase turns with p. Higher frequency t turns faster (more sensitive) but may wrap around.

Like tuning a radio: localize coarsely at low frequency, double the frequency while shrinking the interval (never wrapping), then refine with fresh processors at the highest frequency. Error ≲Qm1​.

Step 71

Collision-free coupling无碰撞耦合

SkimProof techniques

(Optional) Appendix: why we cannot simply pretend there is no overlap.

Rigorous explanation
The collision event {∃i<j:Si​∩Sj​=∅} satisfies so collision-freeness needs N≫n2m2, whereas N≫nm only makes the repeated-access fraction vanish Eq. (492). Since target risks can be exponentially small, coupling failures must be smaller still, so independent-block results cannot be transferred directly.
Plain explanation

The event that all subsets are disjoint; likely once N≫n2m2.

P(∃i<j:Si​∩Sj​=∅)≤(2n​)Nm2​.

A vanishing collision probability is not enough to transfer independent-block results: the target risk may be exponentially small, so the coupling failure must be smaller still. The condition N≳n2m/s in Table I comes from an information argument instead.
